methodological_questions: Defining a suppression-conditional recommended mix from play-by-play and defensive matchup data
Measuring adherence to a dynamic recommended mix (e.g., gap between observed and recommended play-type distributions)
Testing whether adherence predicts win/loss at the game or series level
Controlling for team quality and other confounders
Assessing sample-size adequacy for series-level analysis

historical_evidence.finding: Holdout games where a team's play-type mix is closer to the model's recommended mix score more efficiently: raw gap aligned-deviated +5.18 ORtg; strength-controlled gap +3.27 ORtg (+0.0193 vs -0.0134 PPP residual). Model regret median +25.94 ORtg. n=908 rows, no CI stated. High confidence (0.95). Addresses RQC:RQC-013.

Series-level AVOID share vs winning: game-level rho=-0.19 p=0.008 (inflated n, team-quality confound). Series-level rho=-0.26 p=0.07 (n=50, underpowered; ~80 series needed for p<0.05). Low AVOID-share bin 52.6% vs 25-50% bin 37.0%. Verdict inconclusive.

Execution conformance of observed mix vs recommended plan: avg |delta| on leverage buckets 4.5pp to 24.0pp; 4 of 8 sides best matched opener #3, not rank-1. Single-game horizon, no outcome comparison, CUT and PNR muted for tagger floor. Verdict descriptive.

Audit of LLM adaptation-analysis batch: 706 findings with n<5; series winners LLM-inferred (no actual data lookup); MIA-BOS G7 score invented; point costs are LLM arithmetic. Master '9/10' rule built from LLM inference on inference.

failed_approaches.what_failed: Series-level test of AVOID share vs winning
failed_approaches.why: Confounding by team quality (good teams both disciplined and winning) and insufficient sample size (n=50, need ~80 for p<0.05)

failed_approaches.what_failed: Descriptive conformance assessment without outcome test
failed_approaches.why: MECHANICAL_FLOOR (play types muted for defender), single-game horizon, no win outcome comparison

failed_approaches.what_failed: LLM-based claim that adaptation predicts winning
failed_approaches.why: Artifact: fabricated data, no actual series winner lookup, LLM inference on inference

evidence_establishes: Alignment to a recommended mix (not necessarily suppression-conditional) predicts offensive efficiency at the team-game level (SF-APPM-001).
A related but different adherence metric (AVOID share) was confounded by team quality and underpowered at the series level (SF-CHT-039).
Conformance gap between observed and recommended play-type mixes can be measured, though simple comparisons may suffer from mechanical floors (SF-APPS-017).
Entirely artifact-based claims about adaptation predicting winning have occurred and must be avoided (SF-APPA-008).
evidence_does_not_establish: Whether adherence to a suppression-conditional recommended mix specifically predicts game or series wins.
Whether controlling for team and opponent strength can fully remove the confounding observed in SF-CHT-039.
The optimal method for defining a suppression-conditional recommended mix from the available data.
The practical effect size or statistical power for a win/loss outcome.
own_inferences: A game-level test of the relationship between adherence and winning is more promising than a series-level test because of the much larger sample, but independence violations (games within series, within season) require clustering.

The positive evidence on efficiency (SF-APPM-001) suggests a necessary condition for winning is plausible, but winning adds opposing-team scoring and late-game strategy that may dilute or confound the effect.
If the suppression-conditional recommended mix is derived from the same data used to test it (e.g., in-sample model), lookahead leakage could create an artifactual association.
uncertainties: The precise definition of 'suppression-conditional recommended mix' is not given – it must be operationalised from defensive matchup minutes and play-by-play shooting context.
Whether the model that generates the recommended mix can be trained without using future information or leaking opponent identity.
Sample size for series-level analysis is only 54 series, likely insufficient for adequate power if the effect is small.
Whether the adherence metric will have enough variation to be predictive beyond simple team quality differences.

historical_effect.explanation: SF-APPM-001 demonstrates that mix alignment predicts efficiency, encouraging a test of winning. SF-CHT-039 shows that naive series-level tests of a similar construct are underpowered and confounded, motivating a game-level design with strong team-quality controls. Together they shift the plan from a simple series correlation to a game-level regression with pre-registered adherence metric and lookahead safeguards.

blocking_constraints.text: Better teams may both adhere more to a recommended mix and win more, creating a spurious association that must be controlled with team/opponent strength or fixed effects.
Only 54 playoff series are available; a series-level test would be severely underpowered unless the effect is very large. A game-level analysis is feasible.

If the suppression-conditional recommended mix is computed from future data (e.g., using the whole season to derive defensive suppression parameters), it will incorporate information not available at the time of the game.

prior_work.summary: SF-APPM-001 found that adherence to a recommended mix predicts offensive efficiency, a likely precursor to winning. SF-CHT-039 showed that a naive series-level test of a related adherence metric against winning failed because of confounding and low power. SF-APPS-017 demonstrated feasibility of measuring the conformance gap. The current question extends the evidence by focusing on a suppression‑conditional mix and winning, which remains partly unanswered.

risks.text: Team quality (offensive and defensive talent) could drive both adherence and winning; failing to control for it may produce a small but spurious positive result (as in SF-CHT-039).
Series-level analysis with n=54 is underpowered for a binary outcome; a game-level analysis is needed but may have inflated Type I error if clustering is not handled properly.
If the suppression-conditional model uses defensive matchup data from games that occur after the target game, adherence will be contaminated by the outcome.
The adherence metric (e.g., L1 distance between observed and recommended play-type frequencies) may be noisy within a single game, especially for low-frequency play types.
If many adherence metrics (different distance functions, play-type groupings, suppression definitions) are tested, the primary result must be pre-registered to avoid inflated false-positive rate.

design.estimand: The effect of a team's adherence to its suppression-conditional recommended play-type mix on the probability of winning the game, controlling for team and opponent quality.
design.unit: Team-game observations (each game contributes two rows, one per team).
design.sample: All regular-season and playoff games for the 2022-23, 2023-24, 2024-25, and 2025-26 seasons for which play-by-play and defensive matchup data are complete and the game-end score is available (approx. 4,500 team-game rows).
design.power: Assuming a small effect (odds ratio ~1.1–1.2 per standard deviation increase in adherence), a logistic regression with 4,500 observations and clustered standard errors should provide >80% power at α=0.05; exact power to be verified via simulation with a pre-registered minimal detectable effect size.
design.controls: Team and opponent fixed effects (or random effects) to account for persistent quality differences; control for point spread in-game? Actually, the outcome is win/loss. Could include pre-game team strength proxies (Elo, net rating) to avoid overparameterization. Also control for home-court advantage and rest days.
design.falsification: 1) Test that adherence measured from a random play-type mix (or a mix recommended for a different opponent) does not predict winning. 2) Demonstrate that the estimated effect is not solely driven by the top few teams after residualization.
design.multiplicity: Pre-register a single primary adherence metric (e.g., Euclidean distance between observed and recommended play-type usage frequency vectors, where each component is a play type such as P&R handler, isolation, post-up, etc., curated via factor analysis). All other metrics reported as secondary.
design.decision_rule: Statistical significance at p<0.05 after cluster-robust standard errors (clustered at the team-season level). Report magnitude as odds ratio with 95% confidence interval. Pre-registered threshold for practical significance: OR>1.05 after controls.
design.data_version: NBA 2022-23 through 2025-26 per-game play-by-play, substitution, defensive matchup, and box-score data as described. The suppression-conditional recommended mix model will be trained on pre-2022-23 data (e.g., 2018-19 through 2021-22) to avoid lookahead, with its predictions frozen before any test.

measuring adherence to a dynamic recommended mix
sample size adequacy for series-level analysis

system_prompt:
You are a basketball analytics researcher deciding whether and how a research question should be studied.
You work only from the task statement and the tools listed below. Do not assume facts you have not seen.

The work has two stages, in this order.
Stage 1, retrieval:
1. Read the research objective and the data description.
2. Identify the research concepts and methodological questions the task raises.
3. Retrieve historical evidence by calling retrieve_history.
In stage 1 do not assess the question, predict outcomes or decide. Your only stage-1 reply is the retrieve_history call.
Stage 2, assessment, after the retrieval result is returned:
4. Summarise the relevant historical findings and failed approaches.
5. State what the historical evidence does and does not establish.
6. Assess whether the research question is testable.
7. Identify methodological risks and potential confounders.
8. Make the final research decision.
9. Explain whether and how the historical evidence changed the decision.
The stage-2 output format is given together with the retrieval result.

Evidence rules: keep what a retrieved record states (historical_evidence and failed_approaches, each citing the
identifier of a returned record and its status exactly as recorded) separate from your own inference and from
uncertainty or missing information. Cite only identifiers returned by a tool, and never describe an earlier study that
no tool returned. In some settings retrieval returns no records; then state that no historical evidence was available.

Tools:
- retrieve_history(research_concepts, methodological_questions, query): the prescribed retrieval step. Research question (as posed on 2026-06-16, in the area of defensive suppression and counter strategy (best/avoid)):
Adhering to a suppression-conditional recommended mix predicts winning.

Data available on that date:
- NBA 2022-23 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2023-24 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2024-25 regular season and playoffs
- NBA 2025-26 regular season (complete from 2026-04-13; partial before)
- NBA 2025-26 playoffs (complete from 2026-06-21; partial before)
- Sources: Per-game files from the NBA stats API: play-by-play (action type, sub-type, clock, period, score, player, shot distance and result), substitution rotation intervals, starters, defensive matchup minutes and partial possessions, box-score summary. Derived play-type possession records (initiator, play type, points) in a graph database built from the play-by-play.
- Units available to a study of this question (as recorded): 54 series

Your job is to decide, before any analysis is run, whether this question can be answered with this data, what has already been established about it, which methodological and statistical risks threaten a test of it, and either a pre-registration-quality design or a reasoned recommendation not to proceed.

Stage 1. Reply only with the retrieval call: {"action": "tool", "tool": "retrieve_history", "args": {"research_concepts": ["..."], "methodological_questions": ["..."], "query": "..."}}

So concepts: defensive suppression, recommended mix, adherence, winning. Methodological questions: How to define suppression-conditional recommended mix? How to measure adherence? How to test prediction of winning? Potential confounders: team quality, opponent strength, etc. Risks: sample size (54 series? maybe 54 playoff series? But regular season also available), data sparsity, measurement reliability of derived defensive metrics, etc.

But in stage 1, we just retrieve. We need to list research_concepts and methodological_questions in the args. Also query: a concise description. Let's craft.

Methodological questions: "defining suppression-conditional recommended mix from play-by-play data", "measuring adherence to a dynamic recommended mix", "predicting win/loss from adherence score", "confounding by team strength", "sample size adequacy for series-level analysis".
Query: "suppression-conditional recommended mix adherence predicts winning".

We'll call retrieve_history.

We need to process the retrieval results. We have four records. We need to assess the research question: "Adhering to a suppression-conditional recommended mix predicts winning."

We need to identify research concepts: defensive suppression, recommended mix, adherence, winning. Methodological questions: defining suppression-conditional recommended mix from play-by-play, measuring adherence, predicting win/loss, confounding by team strength, sample size adequacy for series-level analysis.

Now retrieve_history returned four families: FAM:SF-CHT-039, FAM:SF-APPS-017, FAM:SF-APPA-008, FAM:SF-APPM-001. We need to interpret them.

First, FAM:SF-CHT-039: "Series-level AVOID share vs winning (talent confound)". AVOID share maybe related to "avoiding" something; but it's about AVOID share vs winning. It found game-level rho=-0.19 p=0.008 but inflated n and team-quality confound; series-level rho=-0.26 p=0.07 (n=50, underpowered). So a similar question (maybe about a recommended avoidance mix?) but not exactly suppression-conditional recommended mix. It was untestable due to confounding and small sample. So this provides evidence that series-level analysis of a mix adherence vs winning faces sample size and confounding issues.

FAM:SF-APPS-017: "Execution conformance of observed mix vs recommended plan". This is not a hypothesis test; it's descriptive. It measured delta between observed play-type mix and model's recommended opener. No outcome comparison, single-game horizon. So it provides a method for measuring adherence (gap), but doesn't test winning prediction. It has risk MECHANICAL_FLOOR.

FAM:SF-APPA-008: "Audit of overnight LLM adaptation-analysis batch ('9/10 adaptation predicts winning')". Status: artifact. It's about an LLM analysis that was flawed. Not directly relevant, but shows that previous attempt to claim adaptation predicts winning was invalid due to data artifacts. Perhaps cautionary.

FAM:SF-APPM-001: "Play-type mix alignment vs actual PPP (matchup residual)". Status: supported. It found that closer to recommended mix predicts points per possession efficiency, not winning directly. The question was about efficiency (ORtg, PPP residual), not winning games. But it supports that adherence to a recommended mix improves offense efficiency. However, the research question here is about winning, not just efficiency. Winning can be derived but confounding by opponent, other factors.

Now, our research question: "Adhering to a suppression-conditional recommended mix predicts winning." This is more specifically about defensive suppression: a recommended mix that is conditional on suppression (likely some concept of defensive pressure). The data available includes play-by-play, defensive matchup minutes, etc. The "suppression-conditional recommended mix" likely refers to a model that suggests optimal play-type mix given defensive suppression attributes. So adherence to that mix predicts winning. We need to assess testability.

Historical evidence: FAM:SF-APPM-001 supports that alignment to recommended mix (presumably a model's recommended mix based on opponent's defensive scheme) predicts offensive efficiency. That's a similar concept, but not necessarily suppression-conditional. Still, it suggests a possible path: use a model to generate recommended mix given opponent's defensive characteristics (maybe defensive matchups), then compute adherence and correlate with game/series win probability. But winning is a binary outcome at game level or series level. Efficiency might translate to win probability using expected points.

The question could be tested: define the recommended mix (some model output), measure adherence per game or per series, and predict winning (game win or series win). The data includes per-game records for 2022-23 to 2025-26 seasons, with 54 series for playoffs? Actually 54 series total across seasons? The data available: per-game data for regular season and playoffs from multiple seasons. The "units available to a study of this question" states "54 series" - likely playoff series, as each postseason has 4 rounds, 15 series per season? 2022-2026 is 4 seasons, so 4*15=60 series, but maybe 54 due to some incomplete data. So sample size is limited for series-level analysis. Game-level might be many more games: regular season games ~1230 per season, 4 seasons ~4920 games, plus playoffs. So we could do game-level prediction, not just series.

Methodological risks: Confounding by team quality (FAM:SF-CHT-039 showed that). If good teams are both better at adhering and winning, it confounds. So need to control for team strength (e.g., using opponent and team fixed effects, or using efficiency differential). Also, if the recommended mix is derived from the same data (e.g., model trained on past data), there's risk of overfitting and look-ahead bias. The suppression-conditional recommended mix might be defined from data that includes future outcomes; need to be careful with data leakage. The measurement of adherence: how to define "suppression-conditional recommended mix"? If it's a model that uses defensive matchups and play type outcomes, we need to ensure no lookahead. The question might be testable but requires careful design.

The design should specify: estimand is the effect of adherence to recommended mix on win probability (or point differential). Unit: game-level observation, with team-game as row. Sample: all regular season and playoff games from 2022-23 through 2025-26, excluding partial season data? But the data note says 2025-26 regular season complete from 2026-04-13; partial before. So we might include only complete games. For series-level analysis, we could use playoff series. But power may be low.

Risk codes: SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER for series analysis; CONFOUNDING for team quality; perhaps LEAKAGE_LOOKAHEAD if model uses future info; MEASURE_RELIABILITY for adherence metric; MULTIPLE_TESTING if we test many splits.

Given the previous evidence, FAM:SF-APPM-001 supports that mix alignment predicts efficiency, which is a necessary condition for predicting winning. But it doesn't directly test winning. So the question is partly answered for efficiency but not for winning. However, winning is a downstream effect; efficiency predicts winning with high probability, so it's plausible. The main risk is confound.

We need to decide: do_not_proceed? I think a carefully designed test could be done, but the sample size for series is only 54, which is low. Game-level has thousands of observations, but then independence issues (games within series, within season). We could use game-level with clustered errors. The FAM:SF-CHT-039 found sample size issue for series. So game-level could be feasible. However, the research question says "predicts winning". That could mean game win or series win. It doesn't specify. We could test game win. So I'd say testable at game-level with proper controls. But the historical evidence shows that similar question about AVOID share was untestable due to confounding and sample size; but AVOID share might be different. The APPM-001 supported a mechanism.

The record FAM:SF-APPM-001 says status: supported, with high confidence, addresses RQC:RQC-013, which is a research question code. So that's positive. Also FAM:SF-APPS-017 shows a method for measuring conformance gap, but didn't test outcome. So we have methods.

Now, what is the suppression-conditional recommended mix? Probably derived from a model like the one in APPM-001 (which uses "matchup residual" and "model's recommended mix"). So it's alignable.

We need to assess whether the question can be answered with the given data. I'd say p_testable is moderate, like 0.6? But we need to assign probability. I'll think: The data has play-by-play and defensive matchup minutes, so can compute suppression (e.g., defender closeness, shots contested). To define "suppression-conditional recommended mix", we'd need a model that predicts best play type given defensive suppression context. That model must be trained on historical data, with holdout to avoid leakage. Adherence can be computed as distance between observed play-type distribution and recommended distribution per game/possession. Then we predict win/loss (logistic regression) controlling for team/opponent strength, maybe using efficiency ratings. Sample: thousands of regular season games, enough power. Risks: confounding by team quality (can be mitigated with controls), measurement error in adherence, potential overfitting if model uses same-season data. Also, the suppression-conditional recommended mix might be defined using opponent defensive characteristics; but if the same opponent is used in same game, there's mechanical relation (e.g., the recommended mix based on opponent's defensive stats could be collinear with the outcome if opponent's strength is not fully controlled). That's a risk. But still testable.

So p_testable maybe 0.7. But the existence of FAM:SF-CHT-039 suggests that a similar test (AVOID share) was untestable due to confounding. However, AVOID share might be a naive avoidance metric without conditional on suppression. The current question is more nuanced, so maybe confounding is still an issue. I'll assign p_testable 0.6.

Now, for predicted_outcome: The test likely would find a small positive effect, but could be confounded. I'd predict supported with probability 0.4, rejected 0.1 (if null true), untestable 0.3 (due to confounding/sample), artifact 0.1 (if data issues), uncertain 0.1. Sum to 1: 0.4+0.1+0.3+0.1+0.1=1.0.

Decision: I'd say proceed_with_changes, using game-level analysis with opponent strength controls, and pre-registering the model for recommended mix and the adherence metric. So design should specify that.

Now output fields: historical_evidence: list the four records with status as recorded. For FAM:SF-CHT-039: status "untestable". Finding: what it says. FAM:SF-APPS-017: "not a hypothesis test". FAM:SF-APPA-008: "artifact". FAM:SF-APPM-001: "supported". So we list.

Evidence establishes: that alignment to a recommended mix (not necessarily suppression-conditional) predicts offensive efficiency (FAM:SF-APPM-001); that AVOID share vs winning has confounding and low sample (FAM:SF-CHT-039); that adherence gap can be measured (FAM:SF-APPS-017); and that artifact studies can overstate results (FAM:SF-APPA-008).

I'd infer that a game-level test with team fixed effects could potentially isolate the effect of adherence, but still risk overfitting from the recommended mix model.

Uncertainties: The definition of suppression-conditional recommended mix is unclear; the model might not be interpretable; sample of series may be insufficient; risk of lookahead if model uses future data.

Historical effect: changed_decision? I'd say the historical evidence partly changed the decision: The APPM-001 positive result encourages proceeding, while CHT-039 warns about confounding and sample size. So I'd say "yes" and explain that we'd proceed with changes (game-level, controls) based on the evidence.

Now testability: p_testable 0.7, blocking_constraints: CONFOUNDING (talent), SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER for series, maybe MEASURE_RELIABILITY.

I'll add that recommended mix model to be trained on pre-2022-23 data or using cross-validation to avoid leakage.

But we need to detail the design within the given constraints. I'll produce a design that uses per-game data, with adherence measured as the gap between observed play-type distribution and the recommended mix from a model trained on historical data (e.g., 2018-2022). So I'll note that.

Now, output JSON as required.

I'll assemble. Note: predicted_outcome probabilities must sum to 1. I'll set supported:0.45, rejected:0.05, untestable:0.3, artifact:0.1, uncertain:0.1. Slight adjustment.

For FAM:SF-APPS-017, status "not a hypothesis test". For FAM:SF-APPA-008, status "artifact". For FAM:SF-APPM-001, status "supported". For failed_approaches: FAM:SF-CHT-039: what_failed "series-level AVOID share vs winning", why "confounding by team quality and insufficient sample size (n=50, need ~80)". FAM:SF-APPS-017: what_failed "execution conformance measurement without outcome test", why "MECHANICAL_FLOOR, single-game horizon, no outcome comparison". FAM:SF-APPA-008: what_failed "LLM adaptation analysis claiming 9/10 adaptation predicts winning", why "artifact due to fabricated data and no actual data lookup".

I'll avoid FAM:SF-APPM-001 as failed because it succeeded.

Now blocking constraints and risks list both SAMPLE_SIZE_POWER (for series) and CONFOUNDING. I'll include also LEAKAGE_LOOKAHEAD as a risk if model not properly trained.
